title: Transparency, Unanimity & Diversity -- Ch. 15: Ho v. People: Basis for Arrest Warrant
keywords: Section 2, Article III of the Constitution
Roberts Jr. v. Court of Appeals
bail not a bar to objections on illegal arrest
primary_topics: Chapter 15 of 'Transparency, Unanimity & Diversity' -- CJP's account of Ho v. People, the unanimous en banc Decision he wrote holding that a judge may not issue a warrant of arrest on the sole basis of the prosecutor's resolution, because the Constitution commands him to determine probable cause personally and independently.

The middle ground the Decision struck: the judge need not examine the complete records of the preliminary investigation, but must have sufficient supporting documents -- the complaint, affidavits, counter-affidavits, sworn statements or transcripts -- on which to make or at least verify his own finding.

CJP's satisfaction at having reconciled the contentious and divided opinions in Roberts Jr. v. Court of Appeals into a unanimous ruling, and the distinction he drew between the prosecutor's purpose (whether to hold the accused for trial) and the judge's (whether to place him in immediate custody).

The sequel: the wrinkle in Cojuangco Jr. v. Sandiganbayan, where the majority found a waiver of objections through bail and participation, CJP's Dissent that the petitioner's appearance was never voluntary, and the vindication of that Dissent in Section 26 of Rule 114 of the Revised 2000 Rules on Criminal Procedure.
sub_topics: The question posed: on what documents may a judge base an arrest warrant after an information is filed -- the prosecutor's resolution alone, or all the evidence presented at the preliminary investigation?

The facts: on August 8, 1991 the Anti-Graft League of the Philippines complained to the Ombudsman against Doris Teresa Ho, Rolando S. Narciso and others for violating Section 3(g) of RA 3019, which punishes entering into a contract manifestly and grossly disadvantageous to the government whether or not the officer profits.

After preliminary investigation and on Special Prosecution Officer Leonardo P. Tamayo's recommendation, Ombudsman Conrado M. Vasquez authorized the charges on May 5, 1992, and warrants issued, which petitioners attacked as unconstitutional for resting solely on the prosecutor's finding.

The ruling: Section 2 of Article III makes the right against unreasonable searches and seizures inviolable and requires probable cause to be determined personally by the judge after examination under oath of the complainant and witnesses, so the judge may not merely rely on the prosecutor's findings.

The Decision surveyed the post-1987 cases -- Soliven v. Makasiar, People v. Inting, Lim v. Felix, Allado v. Diokno, Webb v. De Leon and Roberts Jr. v. Court of Appeals -- and summarized them in three points.

First: following Inting, the prosecutor determines whether there is reasonable ground to hold the accused for trial, while the judge determines whether there is a necessity for immediate custody so as not to frustrate the ends of justice -- distinct objectives even on the same evidence.

Second: because their objectives differ, the judge must decide independently and must have supporting evidence beyond the prosecutor's bare report; CJP adds the practical suggestion that prosecutors forward enough of the records and evidence to let the judge make that separate finding.

Third: the complete records need not be submitted, since trial courts should not be unduly burdened -- what is required is sufficient supporting documents on which to make an independent judgment or at least verify the prosecutor's findings.

The Decision corrected a possible misreading of Webb v. De Leon, noting that besides the 26-page DOJ panel report the trial court there also had the sworn statements of three witnesses and the petitioners' counter-affidavits before it.

Applied to the case: the Sandiganbayan relied wholly on the graft investigator's resolution, the reviewing prosecutor's memorandum and its own conjecture that the Ombudsman would not have approved without evidence, and had no documents -- not the Contract of Affreightment, the COA-NSC audit report or the counter-affidavits -- so it committed grave abuse of discretion in issuing the warrants ipso facto.
CJP records that he was 'quite happy with the unanimous vote in Ho,' having tried to reconcile the opposing views left by the contentious and divided Roberts Jr. v. Court of Appeals.

The wrinkle: in Cojuangco Jr. v. Sandiganbayan, penned by Justice Leonardo A. Quisumbing, the First Division held that despite the warrant's nullity under Ho the court kept jurisdiction, because the accused had posted bail and participated in the proceedings and so waived his objections.

CJP's Dissent: the petitioner had filed an Opposition to the warrant's issuance on the very ground of inadequate basis, posted bail expressly 'without prejudice' to it, filed a Memorandum in Amplification, moved for reconsideration and sought dismissal after the Ombudsman found no probable cause on reinvestigation -- a continuing, express objection.

He further argued that the conditional arraignment was undertaken solely to accommodate a travel request, that posting bail and seeking leave to travel were special appearances to obtain urgent relief, and that the graft court had 'practically sat on his case' for three years, so treating this as waiver would let courts detain the accused indefinitely.

He proposed remand so the Sandiganbayan could require or receive evidence sufficient for its own probable cause finding -- a procedure he conceded 'may appear cumbersome and unduly harsh on the prosecution' but which the Constitution commands.

The vindication: the Revised Rules on Criminal Procedure abandoned Cojuangco and adopted his Dissent in the new Section 26 of Rule 114, under which an application for or admission to bail does not bar the accused from challenging the arrest, the warrant or the preliminary investigation, provided he raises the objection before entering his plea.

notable_anecdotes: CJP recalls writing Ho as an act of reconciliation -- 'Given the contentious opinions and divided vote in Roberts Jr. v. Court of Appeals, I had tried to reconcile the opposing views' -- and says he is quite happy with the resulting unanimous vote.
He describes the Sandiganbayan's stubbornness in the case, which 'stubbornly stood pat on its position that it had essentially complied with its responsibility' despite having no documents before it.

He recounts the Cojuangco petitioner's 'conditional arraignment,' undertaken in the Sandiganbayan's own words solely to accommodate a request to travel, and subject to being set aside if the reinvestigation exonerated him.
He notes that for three years the graft court 'practically sat on his case,' leaving his objection to the warrant unresolved while he remained bound by its travel restrictions.
He records the final turn -- that the Revised Rules on Criminal Procedure abandoned the Cojuangco ruling and adopted his Dissent as the new Section 26 of Rule 114.

one_paragraph_summary: Chapter 15 of 'Transparency, Unanimity & Diversity' recounted Ho v. People, the unanimous en banc Decision Artemio V. Panganiban wrote to settle what had been confusing jurisprudence on the basis for an arrest warrant. The Anti-Graft League had complained to the Ombudsman against Doris Teresa Ho, Rolando S. Narciso and others under Section 3(g) of RA 3019; Ombudsman Conrado M. Vasquez authorized the charges and the Sandiganbayan issued warrants on the strength of the prosecutor's resolution alone. That, the Court held, violated Section 2 of Article III, which requires probable cause to be determined personally by the judge. Surveying Soliven, Inting, Lim, Allado, Webb and Roberts, CJP summarized three points: the prosecutor decides whether to hold the accused for trial while the judge decides whether immediate custody is necessary; because their objectives differ the judge must decide independently on evidence beyond the prosecutor's bare report; and yet the complete records need not be examined, only sufficient supporting documents such as affidavits, counter-affidavits and transcripts, on which the judge can make or at least verify a finding. He corrected a misreading of Webb, where sworn statements and counter-affidavits had also been before the trial court, and found grave abuse of discretion in a Sandiganbayan that had nothing before it but a resolution, a memorandum and its own conjecture. He noted his pleasure at the unanimous vote, won by reconciling the divided opinions in Roberts. A wrinkle followed in Cojuangco Jr. v. Sandiganbayan, where the majority held that posting bail and participating waived objections to a void warrant; dissenting, he traced the petitioner's continuing objections -- an Opposition, bail posted expressly without prejudice, a Memorandum in Amplification, a motion to dismiss -- and argued that a conditional arraignment sought only to permit travel was no voluntary appearance, that three years of inaction by the graft court made the majority's rule unjust, and that remand was constitutionally commanded however cumbersome. The Revised 2000 Rules abandoned Cojuangco and adopted his Dissent as Section 26 of Rule 114.
